content: Miscarriage is a frequent complication during pregnancy, defined as the spontaneous loss of a pregnancy before 20 weeks of gestation. Progesterone plays a critical physiological role in preparing the uterus for embryo implantation, maintaining uterine quiescence, and suppressing uterine contractions. These functions suggest that progesterone may help prevent the rejection of the embryo. Insufficient progesterone secretion in early pregnancy has been associated with miscarriage, and progesterone supplementation has been used as a treatment for threatened miscarriage to prevent pregnancy loss. This updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 2007 and updated in 2011, evaluates the evidence supporting this practice. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of progestogens in treating threatened miscarriage. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as of August 8, 2017. They also reviewed reference lists of relevant trials. The inclusion criteria were randomized, quasi-randomized, or cluster-randomized controlled trials comparing progestogens with placebo, no treatment, or other treatments for threatened miscarriage in women with singleton pregnancies. Seven trials, involving a total of 696 participants, were included in this review. These trials were conducted in various countries, representing a range of economic classifications. Two trials were conducted in high-income countries (Germany and Italy), four in upper-middle-income countries (Iran, Malaysia, and Turkey), and one in a lower-middle-income country (Jordan). In six trials, all participants met the inclusion criteria, while in the seventh trial, only a subgroup of participants meeting the criteria was included in the meta-analysis. The quality of evidence for the main outcomes was assessed using the GRADE tool, with evidence quality ranging from very low to moderate. The evidence was downgraded due to a high risk of bias in six of the seven trials, a small number of events, and wide confidence intervals for some outcomes. The findings suggest that treatment with progestogens, compared to placebo or no treatment, probably reduces the risk of miscarriage (risk ratio [RR] 0.64, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.47 to 0.87; 7 trials; 696 women; moderate-quality evidence). Specifically, oral progestogen treatment likely reduces the miscarriage rate (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.85; 3 trials; 408 women; moderate-quality evidence). However, vaginal progesterone treatment, compared to placebo, likely has little or no effect on reducing the miscarriage rate (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.21; 4 trials; 288 women; moderate-quality evidence). A subgroup interaction test showed no significant difference in efficacy between oral and vaginal routes of administration. Progestogen treatment, compared to placebo or no treatment, may have little or no effect on reducing the rate of preterm birth (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.44; 5 trials; 588 women; low-quality evidence). Additionally, the effect of progestogen treatment on the rate of congenital abnormalities is uncertain due to very low-quality evidence (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.10 to 4.82; 2 trials; 337 infants). In conclusion, the results of this Cochrane Review suggest that progestogens are likely effective in reducing the risk of miscarriage in cases of threatened miscarriage. However, they appear to have little or no effect on the rate of preterm birth. The evidence regarding the impact of progestogens on congenital abnormalities is highly uncertain due to the limited number of small trials and very low-quality evidence.
